reason: Aborted’s modern brutal death-metal/deathgrind sound is matched closely by both lists. A offers strong scene-adjacent variety: Cattle Decapitation, Hate Eternal, and Origin retain the speed, technicality, and extremity, while Unleashed is more old-school. B has several highly compatible Aborted cuts and a solid Necrotted pick, but the brief atmospheric Interlude is weak as a standalone next-track recommendation, and the list is comparatively redundant.

Tour-Maubourg’s sound sits in warm, jazzy, emotive deep house. List b stays tightly within that lane while expanding across especially compatible artists: Felipe Gordon, Loure, and Chaos in the CBD all share the soulful chords, understated groove, and organic production character. List a has several fitting same-artist selections and dublon is adjacent, but the unknown Boukas track makes it less dependable overall.

Parker’s literate, rootsy pub-rock and new-wave songwriting is well served by both lists. B stays very close through later Parker material, including a fitting acoustic cut, but is entirely same-artist. A offers the more useful path through adjacent power pop, pub rock and British new wave: Crenshaw, Lowe and Miller are particularly natural companions, while the Stranglers track is somewhat darker and less rootsy.

I-Zax sits in the melodic Thai pop-rock lane, and b stays consistently close through same-artist material and adjacent 2000s Thai rock acts such as Bang Kaew, Potato, and Frick. A has strong matches in Basher and I-Zax, but Tattoo Colour is somewhat lighter and funkier, while the Korean (G)I-DLE track is stylistically remote.
I do not know Shirokuma or the seed track well enough to place its sound reliably.

안예은의 극적이고 전통음악 색채가 섞인 어두운 서사성에 ‘출항’과 심규선의 ‘야래향’이 특히 잘 맞는다. A의 나머지는 일부 록·OST·인디 발라드 쪽으로 벗어나지만 분위기상 연결된다. B에서는 ‘난파’가 매우 잘 맞고 ‘나의 오월’도 어느 정도 통하지만, 밝은 ‘여름 좋아’와 현대적인 헤이즈 발라드는 결이 멀다. ‘출항’의 연주 버전도 별도 추천으로는 약하다.
《海洋》是帶有原住民文化氣息、樸素溫暖的民謠作品。A 中陳建年的《故乡普悠玛》最貼近，以莉・高露與 Suming 也延續台灣原住民及土地民謠脈絡；琳誼稍偏流行民謠，PUZZLEMAN 的電子取向較遠。B 的《兰屿之恋》高度契合，低苦艾尚有民謠關聯，但張學友的都市流行情歌明顯不合，整體一致性不及 A。

The seed is bright, summery early-1980s idol pop. “青い珊瑚礁” is an excellent match, but the rest of a moves toward darker rock, anime rock, or later art-pop; the live “少女A” is only broadly adjacent. b stays much closer to Japanese idol kayō/pop, especially Hayami, Oginome, and Honda. The karaoke track is intrinsically weak, but b is still the more coherent continuation.

The seed is a tense, melancholy French crime-film theme with prominent orchestral melody and period soundtrack production. B stays in that world most consistently: de Roubaix’s La scoumoune and Schäfer’s La Victime are especially close, while Cosma and Delerue provide strong French-cinema adjacency. A has several relevant de Roubaix cues, but the Teva material and ballet cue are less specifically aligned, and La chambre bleue is a major stylistic break.

uju’s polished Korean city-pop and synth-pop style is matched closely throughout a_recs: Rainbow note, D2ear, Nahee, and BehindtheMoon all share its bright, smooth, retro-leaning atmosphere. b_recs has useful indie-pop adjacency in Fromm and Kisnue, but Life And Time’s heavier rock character and Peterpan Complex’s alternative orientation make it less consistently suited to the seed.

Tardor’s own studio tracks in a_recs closely match the Valencian/Catalan indie-pop-rock sound, though the live version is a weaker recommendation and Tremp is unfamiliar. b_recs stays largely within the same Valencian indie scene while offering more useful variety: Novembre Elèctric and Smoking Souls are strong adjacent choices, while La Habitación Roja and Corazones Eléctricos are broader Spanish indie-rock fits.
雪沉乐队属于中国旋律化、民乐色彩浓厚的金属语境。B中同乐队的《迷僧》最直接，Mysterain小雨与Voyage in Solitude也延续了民族旋律、氛围感和较阴郁的金属质地；Yaksa和唐朝则只是较宽泛的中国金属关联。A的《云中君》和小雨契合，但有两首无法可靠判断，窒息也偏传统重型，因此B更稳妥。
李明洋屬台語流行情歌路線；A 集中在同一台語歌壇與傷感、苦情的傳統歌謠氛圍，江志豐、袁小迪、陳百潭尤其相鄰，黃文星則較新派。B 多數曲目無法可靠辨識；滿舒克版本的〈My Heart Will Go On〉所屬華語說唱／流行語境與種子歌明顯不合。A 是清楚且一致的選擇。
I do not know “Fairydust” or tokiwa well enough to establish the seed’s sound reliably.
I do not know the seed track or Koa well enough to identify its sound reliably.
I do not know the seed track or artist well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Air Raid’s traditional heavy/speed-metal style makes the same-artist selections strong fits, especially the early, driving “Raiders of Hell.” The second list stays firmly in the modern old-school metal revival: Enforcer is especially close, while Stallion, Morgul Blade, and Sabïre offer compatible speed, melody, and vintage production character. B is preferable because it preserves the fit while providing useful variety beyond Air Raid.
「奏」の温かく切ないピアノ主体のJ-popバラード感に対し、AはSuperfly、ゆず、槇原敬之など歌心の強い同時代のポップスで一貫して近い。Ah Yeah!!は同じスキマスイッチでも勢いが強めだが、音楽的な親和性は高い。Bにも内省的で切ない曲はあるものの、くるりのオルタナ感など質感のずれが目立ち、全体としてAほど直接的ではない。
I do not know this track or Jade well enough to identify its sound reliably.

The Big Hash’s melodic South African hip-hop/R&B style is closely served by b: his own track and FLVME are especially strong scene and sonic matches, with Maraza, K.O and Fifi Cooper retaining a meaningful local rap connection. A is largely obscure to me; Olivia Dean and Wye Oak lean toward soulful pop and indie rock rather than the seed’s rap/R&B setting.

List A stays in Blut aus Nord’s atmospheric, dissonant black-metal orbit: the same artist is an obvious fit, while The Ruins of Beverast, Drudkh, Akhlys, and Misþyrming offer strong adjacent strains of immersive black metal. List B jumps to metalcore, rap metal, big beat/electronica, soundtrack material, and an unknown track, none of which meaningfully matches the seed’s scene or sonic character.

Jean Ritchie’s unadorned Appalachian ballad style makes every selection in a a close fit, though it is narrowly confined to her own catalog. b retains strong traditional-folk continuity through Ritchie, the Kossoy Sisters, Cotten, and Holcomb while offering a more useful tour of adjacent old-time and folk-revival traditions; Henry Thomas is a looser, bluesier connection.

A stays firmly in Energy Flash’s early-90s rave and Belgian techno orbit: Mentasm and Vamp are foundational matches, while Dave Clarke and Dave Angel retain the hard, stark club character. B is mostly far removed—melodic house, jazz/R&B, and psychedelic soul—with only Benny Benassi offering a plausible but much later, more commercial electro-club connection.

Krallice’s dissonant, technical, atmospheric black metal makes all five same-artist selections strong fits, though their stylistic range across releases prevents automatic 5s. The second list pairs the directly related Krallice piece with well-chosen atmospheric and dissonant black-metal peers. It retains the seed’s cold intensity while offering substantially more scene breadth, so it is the more useful recommendation set.
I do not know Chen Guo or the query track well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Joyside’s scruffy, glam-tinged Beijing punk/garage-rock style makes “Silly Girl” an excellent fit and “太空浪子” a strong same-artist match. List A also stays within adjacent Chinese indie, post-punk, and alternative-rock territory, with 木玛 and 动物园钉子户 especially plausible. Most of List B’s generically credited or obscure tracks cannot be placed reliably, so A is the more useful recommendation set.

Iron Mind play tough Australian metallic hardcore. The same-artist hardcore cuts fit closely, while False Reality and Secret World are credible scene-adjacent recommendations. Transforma's electronic drum-and-bass track is a major mismatch, and the alternate/remix-like Speed Experience entry is less useful as a next-song recommendation. Despite two obscure picks I cannot confidently place, a offers the stronger and more exploratory hardcore set.
《九月》是诗性、苍凉而克制的中国独立民谣。B中的《春歌》与种子同属周云蓬，《雾都孤儿》也紧贴张玮玮一脉的西北民谣气质，莫西子诗则延续粗粝、辽阔的诗性；陈粒和谢春花稍偏年轻流行民谣。A里胡德夫、左小祖咒和白羽有相通的人文气质，但整体命中较散，且有一首无法可靠判断。
I do not know SKRY or “Looped Circuit” well enough to characterize the seed’s sound reliably.

The seed is a gentle, sentimental early-2000s Mandopop ballad. A stays close to that sound: Maggie Chiang is especially strong, while Joi Chua and Hou Hsiang-Ting retain the soft, intimate ballad character; Wang Leehom is broader contemporary pop. B has a suitable Joi Chua ballad and a plausible Daniel Chan pick, but Zhou Bichang’s track is stylistically less aligned, and several obscurer tracks are difficult to place confidently.

Shin Yong Jae’s style centers on emotionally intense Korean ballads and drama-OST vocals. Both lists contain strong fits, especially his own ballads and Kim Na Young. EXO’s lighter idol-pop track is a clear stylistic detour, while the piano-version recommendation is limited as an alternate instrumental presentation. Although b has more exact same-artist matches, a offers a useful spread of closely adjacent powerhouse vocalists and OST ballad material, making it the better discovery list.

Tan Dun’s cinematic style combines orchestral writing, prominent strings, and East Asian color. “Eternal Vow” comes from his closely related Crouching Tiger score, while “Sayuri’s Theme” has an especially compatible lyrical cello-led film-score sound. The Perlman, Vengerov, and cello selections share classical string sonorities but lack the same cinematic character. The b tracks are too unfamiliar to place reliably.

The seed is exuberant, rough-edged Japanese rock’n’roll with a strong live-band charge. B stays close to that world: RC’s own 「トランジスタ・ラジオ」 is ideal, Sheena & The Rokkets shares the vintage rock’n’roll attack, and Jun Sky Walker(s) and Lä-Ppisch offer compatible energetic band sounds. 「浅草キッド」 is the clear stylistic detour. A mostly offers polished J-pop or later pop-rock, with much less of the seed’s swagger and grit.

黃小楨’s intimate, understated indie singer-songwriter style makes her own tracks especially strong fits, while 何欣穗 shares the Taiwanese alternative-pop scene and conversational sensibility. A also gets an acceptable Mandarin pop adjacency from JS. B has two excellent scene/artist matches and Summer Salt’s breezy indie-pop is moderately compatible, but the Japanese polished pop of 小松未歩 is less aligned; several obscure candidates limit certainty.

“Galileo” is intimate, literate Irish singer-songwriter folk. Both lists stay broadly nearby, but b has the stronger core: O’Rourke’s “The Stars Over Kinvara,” Paul Brady, and Paddy Casey align well with its acoustic storytelling and Irish scene. Damien Dempsey is rougher and The Waterboys more traditional, but b still offers a coherent, useful range. A includes suitable O’Rourke material, though Maura O’Connell and Paul Heaton are somewhat less exact sonic matches.

Roo'RA's core sound is bright, rhythm-driven mid-1990s Korean dance-pop. List A stays within that contemporary dance and hip-hop scene, especially with Turbo, Kim Sung Jae, and Jinusean. List B's same-artist selections vary more in character; while “날개잃은 천사” is an ideal match, several others are less aligned with the seed's buoyant dance energy. A is also more useful for exploring the surrounding scene.
I do not know La Fuente or this track well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

List A stays firmly in Freaks’ lo-fi indie/surf-post-punk lane: The Drums and Surf Curse are especially close, while The Rare Occasions, Eyedress, and Vundabar share its wiry, youthful indie mood. Most of list B is too obscure for me to place reliably; the identifiable sped-up track is a poor next-song recommendation. A is clearly the useful similar-track set.
I do not know CrowsAlive or this track well enough to establish its sound reliably.

Instinct of Sight belongs to the Hong Kong post-hardcore/metalcore sphere. List b stays consistently within that heavy modern Chinese scene, including a strong same-artist fit and adjacent acts such as 逆流, FUTURE AFTER A SECOND, Inchaos, and Maniac. List a has several plausible mainland metalcore matches, but the anime-associated 横山智佐 track is a major stylistic mismatch, and 穷辛Korsion is unfamiliar.

The seed is a grand, dramatic 1980s Cantonese wuxia TV duet. B contains two especially direct 射鵰英雄傳 companions, plus 葉麗儀’s similarly orchestral classic TV theme, making it the stronger thematic and sonic set. A’s 鐵血丹心 is equally ideal and 甄妮 remains adjacent, but 陳曉東 is from a later Cantopop era and 一生何求 is more restrained urban pop.
I do not know the seed track or Edel Reinklang well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

The seed is an emotionally forceful Mandopop rock ballad built around Princess Ai’s powerful, husky vocal. List A consistently stays near that dramatic 2000s–2010s Taiwanese pop-rock/ballad sound, especially Shin, Power Station, and Miu Chu. Penny Tai is a good match in B and 本多RuRu is broadly adjacent, but several B tracks are too unfamiliar to place confidently, making A the clearly more dependable continuation.

Chill Cole generally makes mellow, polished chillhop and instrumental hip-hop, so the same-artist selections are likely strong stylistic matches. “The Calm Outside” should likewise fit well, while Dylan Sitts is plausibly adjacent in laid-back beat music. I cannot reliably place the other three tracks in b. Despite its limited artist variety, a is the safer and more consistently coherent continuation.

44MAGNUM’s early sound is hard-driving 1980s Japanese heavy metal and glam-leaning hard rock. The same-artist selections in A should fit closely, especially “STREET ROCK'N ROLLER,” but B pairs an apt 44MAGNUM track with strong scene contemporaries REACTION, ANTHEM, and VOWWOW. Ningen Isu is heavier, darker, and stylistically less direct, yet B is the more useful scene-spanning recommendation set.

Gatsby in a Daze sits in China's hazy indie-rock/dream-pop orbit. Railway Suicide Train, Schoolgirl Byebye, and City Flanker are strong scene and production matches, while the same-artist selections in b are naturally close. However, b repeats the query track itself and offers little discovery; a provides several well-targeted neighboring artists, making it the more useful recommendation set.

Jurassic Shark sits in a scrappy Southern California surf/garage/indie-rock lane. The High Curbs, Fake Tides, Junkie, and Wavves all occupy closely adjacent lo-fi, beachy punk territory, while another Jurassic Shark track is naturally well aligned. List A mostly ranges into unrelated country-pop, hip-hop, mainstream pop-rap, and polished alternative rock; the obscure ryster track cannot be placed confidently.

A consistently matches the song’s lush, atmospheric neo-psychedelic and post-punk character: Deerhunter and TOY are especially close, while the Horrors track naturally shares its palette. B has a strong adjacent Temples pick and two mood-compatible Morrissey/Smiths songs, but those are more stripped-down indie jangle; its final selection is stylistically unrelated.

Antzaat’s severe Belgian black-metal style is matched closely by the same-artist cut and by Curse Upon a Prayer, Lhaäd, and Emptiness; Thurisaz is somewhat more melodic and atmospheric. List B stays broadly within extreme or melodic black metal, but ranges farther afield: Infant Annihilator’s technical deathcore is especially mismatched, while Dissection and Illnath provide the strongest black-metal adjacency.

Marf’s style sits in contemporary Hong Kong Cantopop with polished, often dramatic or experimental pop production. List B stays firmly in that current scene: the Marf and Winka tracks are especially close, while sica, Jer and MIRROR remain strong modern Cantopop adjacencies. List A is much looser, mixing older or more conventional ballad-oriented Cantopop, with two tracks I cannot confidently place.

The Immolation selections closely match the seed’s dissonant, oppressive New York death-metal character. List A also stays largely within old-school/brutal death metal: Sinister, Massacre, and Monstrosity are strong scene-adjacent choices, while Korpse is a more modern, slam-oriented mismatch. Despite B’s near-perfect sonic fit, A is preferable because it meaningfully explores related artists rather than offering only more Immolation.

The seed is an intimate, mellow acoustic-pop cover centered on warm vocals. List A consistently follows that character: 陳綺貞 and 王若琳 are especially close, while the stripped-down Billie Jean and Creep covers share its understated cover-song aesthetic. List B is much less reliable; Alaina Castillo has some soft-pop overlap, but the idol-pop track is stylistically distant, and several obscure selections cannot be placed confidently.

1takejay’s style sits in the loose, conversational West Coast street-rap lane. Rucci is an especially close regional and stylistic match, while Capolow, $tupid Young, and Lil Pete remain broadly compatible California rap choices. The 1TakeOcho tracks are too unfamiliar to place honestly, so list B is clearly the more dependable recommendation set.

Both lists suit the track’s warm, sample-rich deep-house character. The Genius of Time selections are especially close in texture and understated groove, but the all-one-artist list is redundant. The second list remains consistently adjacent through dusty, soulful house from Borrowed Identity, Moodymann, Motor City Drum Ensemble and Move D, while offering a much more useful tour of the surrounding scene.

Siwa’s intimate Korean indie-folk style makes “Call My Name” a likely close fit. Lee So Ra is plausibly adjacent in restrained, reflective singer-songwriter mood, while Standing Egg’s piano version is weakened by being an alternate instrumental-style presentation and HYUKOH is only broadly indie-adjacent. I cannot reliably place the specific Korean-titled Siwa songs or JEONGMILLA track, so b is preferable only on the evidence available.

Nancy Whiskey’s sound is rooted in 1950s British skiffle and folk, making her own period recordings and Chas McDevitt’s “Freight Train” highly apt. “Loch Lomond” shares a folk basis but comes from a much later, polished Celtic setting. The Yasuharu Takanashi anime-score selections are stylistically remote; “Bus to Hell” is unfamiliar.

Ceres’ emotional Australian indie/emo-punk style is closely matched by Tiny Little Houses, Dear Seattle, and Bec Stevens; Vera Blue is a softer pop-adjacent stretch. The first three tracks in b are electronic festival/club music and sharply incompatible, though its two Ceres tracks should retain substantial stylistic overlap. List a is clearly the more coherent next-play experience.

The seed is raw, catchy Beijing street punk. A has two excellent same-band matches but is badly disrupted by electronic bass music, alternative rock, and an unrelated classical performance. B stays within the Chinese punk/pop-punk scene: 地下婴儿 and Brain Failure are especially close, while 花兒樂隊 are generally poppier and more playful but still substantially more relevant than A's mismatches.
声音玩具的同团曲最贴近其文学性、渐进铺陈的中国独立摇滚气质。声音碎片、寸铁、野外合作社和木马都处于相邻的本土独立/后朋克谱系；棱镜较偏清亮流行摇滚。青山的老上海时代曲与种子歌的制作和场景距离较远。B整体更稳定，没有明显出戏的一首。
I do not know Eye of Horus well enough to characterize the seed track reliably.

SUPER★DRAGON sits in the dance-heavy Japanese boy-group/EBiDAN sphere. List A stays consistently within that scene, including closely related acts and similarly theatrical pop/rap material. List B has several strong EBiDAN-adjacent choices, but the Finnish metalcore/electronic track by One Morning Left and American hard-rock track by Call Me No One are major stylistic breaks.

Jimmie Vaughan’s sound centers on lean, traditional electric blues and Texas blues guitar. List B stays firmly in that world, ranging from his own work to major blues-guitar and Chicago-blues figures. List A is much less focused: the Yardbirds and Clapton are only broadly adjacent, Ed Bruce is country, and Shaun Martin’s jazz-funk is stylistically distant. The obscure Rolling Stones selection is difficult to place.

ROTH BART BARON’s expansive, pastoral indie-folk/art-rock character is reflected much more closely in A: the same-artist track is strongest, while odol and 折坂悠太 share its thoughtful, organic Japanese indie atmosphere. B is broadly compatible modern Japanese indie, but Suchmos, indigo la End, the band apart, and Vaundy lean more toward groove, polished pop, or mathy guitar rock than the seed’s orchestral folk scale.

“Bulletproof” is sharp, retro-styled electropop with prominent synths and a cool, defiant vocal. A mostly offers modern house/pop-dance tracks: compatible energy, but generally less synth-pop-specific and more club-oriented. B has several melodic electronic-pop selections that may suit the mood, but the TizzyT rap track is a substantial stylistic break, while the nightcore remix is a weak format choice. A is more consistently usable overall.

Ha Hyun Sang’s melodic, emotive indie-pop/rock style is best served by b: “Late Night Movie” is especially close, while I’ll and Hoppipolla share his polished, wistful band sound. LUCY is brighter and more energetic, and KyoungSeo leans toward mainstream ballad-pop, but both remain plausible. A has several fitting same-artist songs, though Parannoul’s noisy shoegaze is a weaker match and the Della Zyr track is unfamiliar.

Both lists suit Estes’s spare, rural Tennessee blues style. B is extremely close sonically, consisting entirely of Estes material, but A offers a more useful journey through adjacent country and piano-blues traditions: Dupree and Lenoir broaden the sound, while Lead Belly and Blind Willie Johnson retain the raw prewar roots atmosphere. That scene-level variety outweighs B’s higher track-by-track fit.

Ngqawana’s music sits in exploratory South African jazz, combining composition, improvisation and indigenous musical language. Both lists remain within that scene, but b is more tightly focused: its Ngqawana suite movements should closely match the seed’s ambitious, elegiac character, while The Jazzanians share his formative jazz context. A offers useful breadth, though Selota and Dyantyis lean more toward song-oriented Afro-jazz and soul.

Jonatan sits in contemporary Polish melodic rap/pop production. Opał is a strong scene-level match, while Białas and Louis Villain also fit that modern Polish hip-hop lane well. Karolina Protsenko’s violin-led instrumental material is a poor match. Too many obscure candidates remain unplaceable for a firm verdict, but b has two clearly suitable picks beyond its mismatch.

Kissing the Pink’s early work sits in the British new-wave/synth-pop world. List B stays there: another closely related Kissing the Pink track plus polished, dramatic 1980s new wave from ABC, Belouis Some, and Classix Nouveaux. List A’s known selections—modern electronic/game soundtrack material and smooth jazz-soul—are far removed in era, songwriting, and production.

Arty Hill’s rootsy honky-tonk and rockabilly-informed country makes the same-artist selections in A reliable fits. B is equally close to that hard-country/Americana world: the Long Gone Daddys are directly connected, while Shaver and Bill Kirchen bring especially strong honky-tonk and country-rock affinities. Pete Bernhard is somewhat darker and folkier, but still compatible. B wins by preserving the barroom roots character while offering a broader, useful path through the scene.

The seed is a restrained, melancholy Korean drama ballad. List A stays consistently in that intimate OST/indie-ballad space: Jung Seung Hwan, Yerin Baek, Heize, and Kim Feel all match its emotional pacing and polished acoustic production. List B has fitting IU and Sondia selections, but KirbLaGoop is a severe stylistic mismatch and the 015B track is not comparably aligned; one candidate is unfamiliar.

Cruel Force plays raw, old-school blackened speed/thrash metal. List B stays firmly in that world: Diabolic Night, Hellripper, Midnight and Desaster all share its aggressive riffing, occult atmosphere and deliberately retro production, with Midnight somewhat punkier. List A is overwhelmingly unrelated; its metal selections come from melodic death metal or modern deathcore rather than the seed’s underground first-wave attack.

Vassline’s metallic Korean hardcore makes its own tracks the closest match in scene, heaviness, and production character. Slant also belongs to Seoul’s hardcore/punk lineage and supplies a credible, raw, aggressive adjacent sound, but its leaner punk attack is less metallic. Despite offering no artist variety, b is preferable because its sonic match is substantially tighter.

The seed is a classic Israeli Hebrew folk song. “Dror Yikra” and “Yerushalayim Shel Zahav” strongly match its Jewish/Israeli folk character, while the Sephardic “La Rosa Enflorece” is a good adjacent traditional choice. “Shma Israel” shares cultural context but is stylistically more modern. The obscure same-name-artist tracks in b cannot be placed reliably, so a is clearly the more useful list.

The seed is theatrical, abrasive Japanese new wave/art rock. A stays close through two strong Yapoos matches and Hikashu’s eccentric avant-new-wave sound; Kiyoshiro is looser, and Hamada is a substantial stylistic miss. B has an excellent Jun Togawa studio-era match and a fitting live Togawa performance, but Akina is only art-pop adjacent, while Ishikawa’s enka and Kai Band’s conventional rock sit much farther away.
I do not know EmptyORio or the query track well enough to establish its sound and judge similarity reliably.
I do not know 熱寫生 or this track well enough to characterize the seed’s sound reliably.

List A consistently matches Kit Chan’s polished Mandarin-pop ballad style: Mavis Hee, Cass Phang, Joi Chua and Stefanie Sun are all credible adjacent singers, while “兄妹” remains close through the same artist. The largely obscure tracks in B cannot be placed reliably, so A is clearly the more dependable similar-track set.

文千岁 belongs to an older Cantonese opera and vintage popular-song tradition. “花开富贵” is the closest match in both lists. B stays more consistently around traditional, festive, and old-style Cantonese repertoire; “今年胜旧年” and 郭炳坚 are especially compatible. A drifts into much later Cantopop and television-theme territory with 譚詠麟, 葉振棠, and Wynners.

The seed sits in the melodic, moody indie-dance/deep-house lane. A is consistently aligned: RÜFÜS DU SOL, Elderbrook, Hayden James, Panama, and Adriatique all share its restrained electronic production and emotive atmosphere. B has excellent matches in RÜFÜS DU SOL and Adriatique, but the Armin van Buuren selections lean toward brighter, more conventional trance and disrupt the flow; Fiona Huang is unfamiliar.

“Traveller” blends Baaba Maal’s Senegalese roots with atmospheric contemporary production. B stays firmly within adjacent African singer-songwriter and roots traditions: Youssou N’Dour and Baaba Maal are especially close, while Mtukudzi, Mabandla, and Rajery retain compatible vocal warmth and acoustic texture. A is mostly disconnected indie, folk-rock, jazz, and art-soul; even its moodier selections do not share the seed’s West African rhythmic and vocal character.

The seed is an elegant, wistful early-1980s Cantonese ballad. B stays consistently within classic Cantopop’s restrained, nostalgic duet-and-ballad tradition; the live 徐小鳳 recording is a slight format drawback but still musically close. A has strong matches in 問我 and 似是故人來, yet 餓狼傳說 is much more forceful dance-pop, while 讓我坦蕩蕩 is comparatively upbeat.

The seed is a warm, nostalgic late-1970s Taiwanese campus-folk standard. List B stays close to that world: 羅大佑 and 葉佳修 strongly match its acoustic, pastoral nostalgia, while Julie Sue and 潘安邦 remain adjacent. List A includes the seed itself and a fitting 潘安邦 song, but the mainland vocal-song selections and later pop of 跟着感觉走 are less specific to its campus-folk character.

Darkest Horizon's cinematic, symphonic melodic death metal makes the same-artist selections exceptionally close fits. The second list remains firmly in melodic death metal, with Mors Principium Est, The Halo Effect, Children of Bodom, Whispered, and Engel offering compatible riffing and intensity, though generally less orchestral. Despite slightly weaker individual matches, b is the more useful recommendation set because it explores several adjacent artists rather than only returning Darkest Horizon.
I do not know the seed track or 昴宿 Pleiades well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Both lists stay within dance-oriented second-generation K-pop. A has two especially close matches in EXID’s similarly brassy “덜덜덜” and Girl’s Day’s sultry “Something,” but its 4minute and Apink cuts are less aligned. B is more consistently geared toward the seed’s sexy, catchy club-pop character: Stellar and Brave Girls are excellent scene and mood matches, while Badkiz and 2NE1 preserve the bold energy.

The seed is a wistful, narrative-driven Mandarin pop ballad with a classic late-80s/early-90s feel. List B consistently stays in that intimate, nostalgic world: 陳淑樺 and 孟庭葦 are especially close, while 娃娃 herself and the older folk-pop selections remain compatible. List A contains several tracks I cannot place confidently; 徐小鳳 is broadly adjacent but the live presentation is less ideal, and 鳳凰傳奇’s 刘三姐 is stylistically far removed.

Yokota’s music sits in a delicate ambient/electronic space. B consistently follows that atmosphere: Tobiume is an especially close same-artist fit, while Biosphere, Meitei, and naran ratan offer suitably hushed, textural neighbors. Mort Garson is more vintage and whimsical but still plausible. A contains two unknowns and veers toward turntablism and soundtrack pop; only Yokota’s Blue Sky And Yellow Sunflower seems strongly aligned.
I do not know the seed track or artist well enough to judge its sound without inferring from titles.

Cavour’s style is Bolivian/Andean charango-centered folk. The Cavour-heavy b list is likely the closest sonically, while Centellas and Los Calchakis also sit naturally in that instrumental Andean tradition; Violeta Parra is broader vocal nueva canción, so less exact. Despite b’s stronger direct fit, a is the more useful recommendation set because it reaches into the surrounding scene rather than offering only the seed artist. Perri is unfamiliar.

The seed is polished, romantic contemporary pop with an intimate singer-songwriter feel. List A stays consistently in that lane: bright, melodic, affectionate pop with similarly clean production, and the elijah woods track is especially close. Finding Hope offers a compatible dreamy bedroom-pop mood, while Tom Frane is broadly adjacent, but several List B tracks are too unfamiliar to place confidently. List A is the more dependable continuation.
香坂みゆきの都会的な80年代歌謡・シティポップ寄りの作風には、同時代の女性アイドル／アーバンポップを揃えたbが明確に近いです。国分友里恵や芳本美代子、工藤夕貴は特に時代感と艶のあるポップ感が合います。aは来生たかお以外、フォーク／ニューミュージックや90年代ポップへ離れ気味です。

Dakis belongs to polished Greek pop and light-laiko of the 1960s–70s. List B stays closer through Dakis recordings and Hatzinasios’s strongly related period songwriting, though “I Who Have Nothing” is a less specific fit and the Stereomatic track is unfamiliar. List A has suitable vintage Greek-pop choices, especially Voskopoulos, but Malamas is from a later, earthier entechno tradition and Morfi is more retro-modern.

Kahara’s style sits in polished 1990s Japanese pop, especially the Tetsuya Komuro orbit. The GLAY pick is adjacent era-wise but more rock-oriented; the other b tracks strongly match that J-pop/dance-pop scene and production style. A is largely unrelated, spanning folk and contemporary experimental pop, with two tracks I cannot confidently place.

The seed sits in DDG's Chengdu-rooted Chinese trap/hip-hop lane. B is anchored by two well-matched DDG cuts, especially “武侯区,” with Asen also fitting the contemporary Southwestern rap scene; Pharaoh is broader stylistically. A has solid adjacent picks from Xie Di and Narchy Wolf, but the live Pissy and AnsrJ recordings are less suitable as next-track recommendations.

Santiago Feliú’s intimate, harmonically adventurous Cuban nueva trova style is matched very closely throughout A, including strong scene links through Noel Nicola and Vicente Feliú. B begins well with Feliú and adjacent canción de autor/nueva canción choices from Aute and Milanés, but Chavela Vargas and Facundo Cabral move toward older ranchera/Latin American folk traditions with a noticeably different vocal and production character.

The seed is Sibelius’s serene, devotional hymn tune. List A better preserves its sacred choral atmosphere: Fauré’s Sanctus and Sibelius’s Rakastava are especially strong, while Mahler’s resurrection chorus is grander but related. List B stays close to Sibelius and Finnish Romanticism, yet mostly substitutes instrumental chamber and concerto writing; Valse triste shares the reflective melancholy, but the violin concertos are much more dramatic and virtuosic.

Hillbilly Rawhide's mix of psychobilly, country, rockabilly and punk makes the same-artist selections consistently close, especially the rough, road-driven material. Matanza is an excellent Brazilian country-hardcore neighbor, and Velhas Virgens has compatible boozy rock attitude, but Ludov's polished indie pop is stylistically remote. With Confraria da Costa uncertain, a is the more reliable set despite offering less discovery.
I do not know BG8LOCC or this track well enough to characterize the seed's sound reliably.

The seed is a Marathi Ganesh aarti with traditional devotional singing and instrumentation. A contains one clearly unrelated pop song, while its Ravindra Sathe selections are not necessarily devotional despite the vocal continuity; “He Gajaanan Baba” is the strongest match. B offers two close contemporary bhajan choices and a broadly compatible devotional film song, though “Tim Tim Timbali” is less aligned and “Dwadas Adhaya” is unfamiliar.
I do not know the seed track or Seoul Music Ensemble well enough to identify its sound reliably.

Stompin' Bird sit in Japan's melodic punk scene, and list A stays tightly within that fast, upbeat, guitar-driven world: Over Arm Throw, HOTSQUALL, and locofrank are especially natural neighbors. List B has solid punk choices in STANCE PUNKS and Hump Back, but The 50 Kaitenz is more garage rock, while Humbert Humbert's acoustic folk is a substantial stylistic mismatch.
I do not know the seed track or Itoko Toma well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

LINION’s sound centers on smooth Taiwanese neo-soul, R&B, and laid-back groove. “Room 335” and “想不起你的名字” are direct fits; Osean and It’s Your Fault also sit comfortably in the adjacent indie/R&B scene. Karen Mok is broader Mandopop but plausible, while Eric Chou and the known generic pop-ballad material are weaker stylistic matches. List a offers the stronger, more consistently groovy scene connection.

Stilz sits in cinematic, retro-futurist synthwave. A stays especially close: VHS Dreams, NightStop, and Stilz’s own Starcrash share the nocturnal driving atmosphere and period-styled production, while Absolute Valentine and Timecop1983 remain strong adjacent fits. B is consistently synthwave-related, but Fury Weekend and Perturbator lean heavier and more aggressive, and Jasper Byrne’s game-score character is somewhat less exact.
I do not know the seed track or Yoga Motion well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Plamina’s acoustic-cover style makes “Truly Madly Deeply” an especially close match, while Grace George’s acoustic ballad treatment is also clearly adjacent. List a ranges into contemporary R&B, jazz, and unrelated singer-songwriter territory; only “wonderful u” plausibly shares the intimate, gentle mood. Several obscure cover versions cannot be placed confidently.

The seed belongs to the traditional German North Sea shanty-choir style. Both lists contain strong maritime choral matches, but B is especially focused, with a classic shanty medley and several closely fitting songs by Frische Brise. A’s Santiano unplugged track is more modern folk-rock, while Curd Jürgens’ Reeperbahn song is maritime-adjacent entertainment rather than a close choral match.
I do not know the seed track or Shennumbanine well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

“Axe Crazy” is raw, fast early-NWOBHM. Jaguar’s “The Fox” and “Dutch Connection” are especially close, while the other identifiable Jaguar cuts remain stylistically compatible. The Jagúar entry is unclear. List b is stronger holistically: Hollow Ground and Tysondog stay firmly in the same underground British metal scene, Girlschool is a credible adjacent match, and Ostrogoth preserves the traditional speed-metal energy while adding useful variety.

Huun-Huur-Tu’s Tuvan throat-singing, drones, bowed strings and steppe-folk character are matched directly by their other songs and very closely by Yat-Kha and Alash Ensemble; Egschiglen and Altai Khangai provide strong Mongolian folk adjacency. Although b has four excellent same-artist fits, the unfamiliar opening track is uncertain and the list is comparatively narrow. A offers a more useful tour of the closely related Tuvan and Mongolian scene.

Kane’s spare, rootsy Americana is closely matched by Rayna Gellert and fellow Dead Reckoning songwriter Kevin Welch, while the three Kane selections should retain the intimate country-folk character. Gurf Morlix is an especially strong fit in b, but Neal Casal, Old 97’s, and Lucero lean progressively more toward rock-oriented alt-country. The live cuts in a remain normal performances rather than redundant versions, and a is more consistently aligned overall.

250’s track sits in a retro Korean dance-pop/electronic world with nostalgic, stylized production. Red Glass is the strongest A match; Parov Stelar and Bellaire share vintage dance textures but come from different electro-swing/house scenes, while Bad Omens is plainly unrelated. B repeats the seed itself, but Risso is strongly adjacent and Clazziquai and XXX retain meaningful Korean electronic connections. Despite the redundant first slot, B is the more coherent set.

Niaz Nawab's own tracks are the safest matches for his contemporary Persian alternative/pop-rock style, and the title-script variant appears to be the seed itself. List A therefore has several close matches, though the Erwin Khachikian tracks are hard to place confidently. List B stays broadly within Iranian alternative music, but Namjoo, Rana Mansour, and Radio Tehran each bring a more distinct stylistic character.
脏手指属于粗粝、戏谑的中国朋克/车库摇滚语境。B以同乐队歌曲及假假條、Joyside、回春丹等相邻的地下摇滚和朋克作品为主，整体场景与气质高度贴合；郭顶则偏精致流行。A中林子祥和满舒克明显脱离该声音，RAMBO GANG至多有些青年亚文化关联，另两首无法可靠判断。

Quarterback’s style sits in Taiwanese alternative/indie rock with an emotive, melodic band sound. A stays consistently within that ecosystem: Mary See the Future, Hello Nico, Tolaku, and Sweet John are credible adjacent picks, while Quarterback itself is especially close. B has one excellent same-artist match, but otherwise wanders into Mandopop/folk and a more abrasive Shanghai underground-rock context; one track is too unfamiliar to place.

Marc Robine belongs to the French chanson and traditional-song world, with a strong historical, political and anarchist repertoire. List A closely follows that character through protest chanson, revolutionary song, maritime folk and French folk revival artists. List B mostly offers stylish French pop, soundtrack music and newer indie chanson; the shared language does not compensate for the very different instrumentation, cultural setting and mood.

“Bella” sits in the early-2010s melodic, vocal-tinged deep-house lane. Both lists largely match its warm basslines, restrained club pulse, and moody polish. List A is especially close but leans heavily on Finnebassen’s own catalog; B offers stronger scene-level discovery through Miguel Campbell, Karmon, and Teenage Mutants while retaining the right atmosphere. I cannot confidently place the Bukka & Molinari track.

The seed turns Kawai’s ceremonial Ghost in the Shell choral theme into a large-scale EDM remix. List A at least targets contemporary festival/electronic production, though its known selections lack the seed’s ominous Japanese cyberpunk atmosphere. List B sits around Japanese doujin/vocal music, but that scene connection does not reproduce the remix’s heavy EDM impact, orchestral tension, or chant-driven mood.

“Aloha” sits in breezy, melodic French tropical/electronic pop. B stays firmly in that lane: Tez Cadey and Petit Biscuit are especially close in sunny atmosphere and polished production, while Møme is naturally aligned. Feder and Montmartre remain compatible French electronic-pop choices. A has some dreamy mood overlap through Cannons, DEAMN, and Rhye, but Ash Code’s darkwave and Camera Obscura’s indie pop are stylistically remote.

A stays firmly in polished British synth-pop and New Romantic territory. “When Smokey Sings” is an especially strong same-artist fit; “Relax” and “Too Shy” share the glossy early-80s production, while the Pet Shop Boys track is stylistically related but much later. B is dominated by modern hip-hop and unrelated contemporary pop, far removed from ABC’s orchestral, theatrical dance-pop sound.
白虹屬於民國時期上海時代曲語境。A前三首都貼近同代女歌手、爵士化流行曲與老唱片質感，但謝雷和田震分屬明顯更晚且不同的流行風格。B除胡德夫的1970年代台灣民歌取向嚴重偏離外，其餘周璇、吳鶯音及兩首白虹作品都非常貼合，因此整體更可靠。
I do not know the seed track or Fırat Durak well enough to identify its sound and judge similarity reliably.

Ayrapetyan’s repertoire centers on Armenian piano music and folk-rooted miniatures. B stays consistently within solo classical piano: the Ayrapetyan selections are especially close in cultural and compositional character, while Buniatishvili’s chanson arrangement, Mussorgsky, and Scarlatti are broader but still plausible. A is mostly unfamiliar and appears disconnected; the known Mandopop/rap rendition of “My Heart Will Go On” is a clear mismatch.

“So What” is polished mid-2000s Southern pop-rap/R&B. B largely stays in that lane: Ciara and Chingy are especially close in era, crossover production, and relationship-focused mood, while Lil’ Flip also fits the Southern rap context. Kelly Rowland is somewhat adjacent; Salt-N-Pepa is much too early. A’s identifiable tracks lean indie pop or alternative pop and do not match the seed’s crunk-era rap/R&B character.
I do not know SADOG or this track well enough to identify its sound reliably.

李佳隆’s melodic Chinese hip-hop style is well served by the first list: his own track is closest, while 黃旭, GALI, and 艾熱AIR remain within the adjacent Mandarin rap scene, though with varying melodic character. I cannot reliably place the obscure tracks in the second list, so the first is the only defensible recommendation set.

7SENSES’ polished, performance-driven C-pop/electropop style is best matched by “U Know,” while SNH48 and Yu Yan also stay close to its idol-pop scene and sleek production. List b has relevant SNH48/BEJ48 connections, especially “Show,” but several solo or live selections are less direct sonic matches, and “9to9” is unfamiliar.

Vincy Chan’s style sits in polished mid-2000s Hong Kong Cantopop, especially melodic female-led pop ballads. A stays closer to that scene through Vincy, Sherman Chung, and Mag Lam; Sammi Cheng is broader-era adjacent, while Leo Ku’s live track is less direct. B has a strong fit in Jade Kwan and some compatible Chinese pop, but the two Steven Ma selections are weaker stylistic matches.

The seed is earthy 1970s Japanese blues. “シカゴ・バウンド” is an excellent same-band blues match, and BEGIN’s “恋しくて” shares its soulful, blues-rooted melancholy. The Folk Crusaders are broadly adjacent Japanese roots music, while OLD DAYS TAILOR is much later and cleaner. List a consists of later novelty/soundtrack material by the same band; despite the familiar vocals and playing, its theatrical character is substantially removed from the seed.

Lianie May’s polished Afrikaans pop-country style makes all of a’s same-artist selections plausible, though their exact moods may vary. B stays in the contemporary Afrikaans pop/sokkie scene: Brendan Peyper is especially close, while Jay and 4Werke are strong adjacent choices; Jo Black is somewhat more adult pop-rock. B is preferable because it preserves the scene and dance-friendly character while offering useful variety.

The seed is bright, jangly early-80s American power pop associated with the college-rock scene. List A consistently matches that melodic guitar sound: Let's Active itself, The Records, Robyn Hitchcock, Love Tractor, and later power-pop heirs Sloan. List B mostly offers unrelated synth-pop, dance-pop, hard rock, and Celtic folk-punk; shared 1980s context does not make those close sonic matches.

Sinmara’s dissonant, atmospheric Icelandic black metal makes every same-artist selection an excellent sonic fit. But b is the stronger recommendation set: Almyrkvi and Svartidauði are especially close scene companions, while Skáphe shares the oppressive dissonance and Mgła remains compatible black metal despite a more melodic, driving approach. It preserves the seed’s darkness while offering meaningful variety.

Catie Curtis's intimate contemporary folk and singer-songwriter style is well served by Deb Talan, Antje Duvekot, and Gretchen Peters; the Secret Sisters are somewhat more roots-country and produced. The Curtis-heavy list likely offers several very close fits, though “Radioactive Wild Boar” is unfamiliar and the Bacharach cover is less characteristic. List A wins by maintaining the acoustic storytelling mood while offering useful variety across the same folk scene.

Suyano sits in the polished mid-2010s progressive/big-room festival-house lane. A consistently matches that sound: Shockwave and Dreamin are especially close, while JAGGS, Sultan + Shepard, and Radiology remain strong EDM neighbors. B has suitable melodic festival-house choices from Manse, Arston, and WildVibes, but two tracks are too unfamiliar to place confidently, making A the more dependable result.

Garion’s style is foundational, lyric-heavy Korean underground hip-hop with a rugged old-school character. Infinite Flow is the strongest scene match in A, and Primary is adjacent, but Jaurim is stylistically unrelated. B stays much more consistently within Korean hip-hop: Garion, YDG, and Onesun suit the seed’s era and rap focus, though PSY’s intro and Outsider’s faster, more theatrical style are less exact.
I do not know the seed track or Effie well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Sandee Chan’s art-pop/indie singer-songwriter character is best matched by her own “幻覺” and Yang Naiwen’s cool, alternative-leaning Mandopop. A has a strong same-artist pick in “海邊,” but the acoustic Natural Q track is only broadly adjacent, while Yang Hesu’s rap is a major stylistic break. B drifts toward conventional vocal-ballad pop later, yet remains more coherent overall.

List A stays firmly within Zoé’s Mexican alternative/psychedelic rock orbit: Enjambre, León Larregui, La Castañeda, and San Pascualito Rey all share relevant mood, scene, or dramatic texture, while “Soñé” is especially close. List B begins with unrelated electronic tracks; the live Zoé cover has some atmospheric fit but is less suitable than an original studio track. The final two Zoé titles are too obscure to place reliably.
“小半”是细腻、克制而略带忧郁的华语民谣。A中的陈粒、老狼、阿肆和宋冬野都处于相近的独立民谣/唱作人语境，尤其《斑马，斑马》在氛围与编配上很贴近。B中的郑润泽两首尚有情绪化流行唱作的联系，但整体更偏当代流行；人間椅子的重型摇滚则明显不合。
I do not know Pay4n or the query track well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Lujiachi’s work sits in a dark, highly designed electronic space, so the same-artist selections and Dirty K remix are likely close in production character. Meuko! Meuko! and Scintii are strong Taiwanese experimental-electronic neighbors, but the other b picks are unfamiliar or less clearly aligned, making a the more dependable continuation despite its narrowness.

The Hertz sit in Hong Kong indie rock/pop, and list A consistently explores adjacent Chinese-language indie acts: Schoolgirl Byebye, Everfor and WHIZZ are especially plausible scene and production matches. Yoyo Sham is somewhat softer and more art-pop leaning. List B has three strong same-artist choices, but the conservatory rendition of “沁园春·长沙” is a severe stylistic break, and “珍妮的潮汐” is unfamiliar. A is the more coherent and exploratory recommendation set.

Both lists stay close to the seed's late-70s/early-80s American punk attack. A offers highly compatible Dead Kennedys material, though “Advice From Christmas Past” is a less direct musical match. B pairs an excellent same-artist choice with adjacent California punk, hardcore, and eccentric punk-scene cuts. Its broader scene coverage makes it the more useful recommendation set despite a slightly uneven Dickies pick.

Cryfemal’s raw, depressive Spanish black metal character makes all five same-artist selections exceptionally close fits. List A retains one direct Cryfemal match, then explores genuinely adjacent raw/depressive black metal through Dodsferd and Xasthur; Despondent Moon and Trhä are somewhat more atmospheric and stylistically removed. Despite B’s stronger track-by-track fit, A is the more useful recommendation set because it opens up the surrounding scene rather than offering only the seed artist.

ダウト’s visual-kei rock style is strongly served by A: vistlip, メガマソ, and DIAURA are close scene matches, while MIYAVI is a broader but still plausible rock connection. B starts well with D and DaizyStripper, then veers sharply into idol-pop and novelty-oriented material with little sonic relationship to the seed.

The seed is a polished, melancholy Mandopop breakup ballad. A consistently stays in that intimate 2000s–2010s sentimental-pop lane: Rachel Liang, Freya Lim, Rynn Lin and Aska Yang are all compatible, though the live recording is less ideal. B’s Michael Wong selections fit very well, especially the closely related warm ballad style, but several obscure tracks cannot be placed reliably, making A the stronger complete recommendation set.
I do not know the seed track or Shubhangi Joshi's music well enough to judge its sound reliably.

The seed is mournful, spacious European film-score chamber music. Karaindrou’s Adagio, El vals, and Tango of Love preserve that austere lyricism particularly well, while Badalamenti is a strong atmospheric neighbor; Woodkid is more modern and production-heavy. List A has excellent Karaindrou and Preisner choices, with Reboutsika adjacent, but Gokcin and Farjad are looser neo-classical/world-instrumental matches.
I do not know “IHATOV” or lang well enough to characterize the seed’s sound reliably.
I do not know the seed track or Kärntner Viergesang well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Yamanaka’s style is modern, technically agile piano-trio jazz. A stays consistently within Japanese jazz and jazz-fusion: Terai and Matsumoto are especially plausible neighbors, while Casiopea and Honda lean more toward electric fusion. B has two strong same-artist choices, but the sprawling Alchemist yacht-rock mix is badly mismatched and Yamashita’s polished city-pop reading is only broadly adjacent. A is the more coherent next-track set.
I do not know the seed track or Selvageria well enough to characterize its sound reliably.

Kawa’s rootsy, reggae-inflected Yunnan folk-rock is best matched by their own track and Hanggai’s forceful folk-rock drinking song. Li Naluo also brings a strong southwestern ethnic-folk connection. The XTX selections are credible Chinese rock neighbors but less culturally and rhythmically specific; Skaraoke’s ska/reggae adjacency fits only partially, and two obscure candidates are difficult to place.

The seed is glossy, forceful early-2010s pop with pop-rock bite and a big vocal hook. List B stays firmly in that lane: Demi and Taylor are especially close, while Nick Jonas, Avril Lavigne, and Becky G retain the punchy mainstream-pop appeal. List A has a couple of plausible pop connections, but Endlessly is softer and the acoustic Christopher track lacks the seed's production impact; two selections are unfamiliar.

Totenwache plays raw, traditional German black metal, so the same-artist selections in b are extremely close fits but make for a narrow result. A retains one direct match and adds credible German black-metal neighbors: Mavorim and Runenwacht are especially aligned, while Non Est Deus and the more polished, melodic Dark Fortress are somewhat less exact. A is the more useful recommendation set despite b’s stronger track-by-track similarity.
譚炳文的老派粵語歌／粵曲背景，使鄭錦昌的懷舊粵語小曲最貼近；羅嘉良和葉麗儀尚有復古港樂連結。A中的任劍輝偏向更純粹的粵劇，蔡琴則是國語懷舊歌；張學友與草蜢等現代粵語流行製作距離較大。B因有一首極強的同場景推薦而略勝。
